questiontext.text:
Refer to the diagrammatic representation of the stomatal apparatus shown below:

In the stomatal apparatus of dicotyledonous leaves, which of the following statements correctly describes the structural characteristics of the guard cells and subsidiary cells?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand the composition of the stomatal apparatus
The stomatal apparatus comprises the central stomatal aperture (pore), a pair of enclosing guard cells, and the surrounding specialised epidermal cells called subsidiary cells.

Step 2: Examine the morphology and wall thickenings of guard cells
In dicotyledons, guard cells are bean-shaped (kidney-shaped). The outer walls facing away from the stomatal pore are thin and elastic, whereas the inner walls facing towards the stomatal pore are highly thickened and inelastic.

Step 3: Analyze the cellular contents and function of guard cells
Unlike typical epidermal cells which lack chloroplasts, guard cells possess functional chloroplasts. Changes in turgor pressure within the guard cells drive the opening and closing of the stomatal aperture.

Step 4: Analyze subsidiary cells
Subsidiary cells are specialised epidermal cells located in immediate contact with the guard cells, aiding in the mechanics of stomatal movements.

Step 5: Conclude the correct anatomical description
The accurate structural description is that guard cells possess chloroplasts, thin outer walls away from the pore, and highly thickened inner walls facing the stomatal pore.

answer.text: Guard cells possess dumb-bell shapes with uniformly thin cellulose walls and completely lack chloroplasts.
Guard cells possess thin inner walls towards the stomatal pore and heavily thickened outer walls away from the pore.
Guard cells possess chloroplasts, thin outer walls away from the pore, and highly thickened inner walls facing the stomatal pore.
Subsidiary cells are specialised vascular elements located in the mesophyll that directly regulate transpiration.

questiontext.text:
Refer to the diagrams illustrating three primary types of vascular bundles labelled (a), (b), and (c):

Which of the following options correctly identifies the vascular bundle types (a), (b), and (c) along with their respective anatomical features and organ of occurrence?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand radial vascular bundles
In radial vascular bundles, xylem and phloem are arranged in an alternate manner along different radii. This configuration is the diagnostic hallmark of primary roots in angiosperms.

Step 2: Understand conjoint closed vascular bundles
In conjoint closed vascular bundles, xylem and phloem lie jointly along the same radius with phloem located towards the exterior, but without any intrafascicular cambium between them. Lacking meristematic activity, they cannot undergo secondary growth, which is characteristic of monocotyledonous stems and leaves.

Step 3: Understand conjoint open vascular bundles
In conjoint open vascular bundles, an intrafascicular cambium strip is present between the outer phloem and the inner xylem along the same radius. The presence of cambium confers the ability to generate secondary xylem and secondary phloem, which is characteristic of dicotyledonous stems.

Step 4: Synthesize the correlations
Structure (a) represents a radial bundle characteristic of roots; structure (b) represents a conjoint closed bundle characteristic of monocotyledonous stems lacking cambium; structure (c) represents a conjoint open bundle characteristic of dicotyledonous stems possessing intrafascicular cambium.

Step 5: Conclude the final match
The correct identification corresponds to: (a) Radial bundle in roots with xylem and phloem on different radii; (b) Conjoint closed bundle in monocot stems lacking cambium; (c) Conjoint open bundle in dicot stems possessing intrafascicular cambium.

answer.text: (a) Radial bundle in roots with xylem and phloem on different radii; (b) Conjoint closed bundle in monocot stems lacking cambium; (c) Conjoint open bundle in dicot stems possessing intrafascicular cambium.
(a) Conjoint open bundle in dicot stems; (b) Radial bundle in roots; (c) Conjoint closed bundle in monocot stems.
(a) Conjoint closed bundle in leaves; (b) Conjoint open bundle in dicot roots; (c) Radial bundle in monocot stems.
(a) Radial bundle in dicot stems; (b) Conjoint open bundle in monocot roots; (c) Conjoint closed bundle in leaves.

questiontext.text:
Refer to the transverse section of a dorsiventral (dicotyledonous) leaf shown below:

Based on the vertical section of a typical dorsiventral (dicotyledonous) leaf, which of the following statements is correct regarding the internal tissue organization?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand mesophyll differentiation in dorsiventral leaf
In a dorsiventral (dicotyledonous) leaf, the ground tissue between the upper (adaxial) and lower (abaxial) epidermis is termed mesophyll. It is differentiated into two distinct regions: palisade parenchyma and spongy parenchyma.

Step 2: Characterize palisade parenchyma
Palisade parenchyma is situated towards the upper (adaxial) surface and consists of columnar, elongated cells arranged vertically and parallel to each other with minimal intercellular spaces.

Step 3: Characterize spongy parenchyma
Spongy parenchyma is situated beneath the palisade cells towards the lower (abaxial) epidermis, consisting of loosely packed oval or rounded cells with numerous large intercellular spaces and air cavities.

Step 4: Analyze stomatal distribution and vascular bundle orientation
The abaxial epidermis generally bears significantly more stomata than the adaxial epidermis. The vascular bundles in veins are surrounded by a compact bundle sheath, with xylem oriented towards the adaxial side and phloem towards the abaxial side.

Step 5: Conclude the valid anatomical statement
The correct statement is that the mesophyll is differentiated into adaxially placed vertically elongated palisade cells and loosely arranged abaxial spongy parenchyma with large intercellular spaces.

answer.text: Palisade parenchyma is located towards the abaxial epidermis and consists of loosely arranged rounded cells with large air cavities.
Stomata are completely absent on the abaxial epidermis and predominantly restricted to the adaxial epidermis.
The vascular bundles lack any sheath of cells and possess phloem oriented towards the adaxial surface.
The mesophyll is differentiated into adaxially placed vertically elongated palisade cells and loosely arranged abaxial spongy parenchyma with large intercellular spaces.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMY_OF_FLOWERING_PLANTS_MCQ_Q04 - Comparative histological features of angiosperm stems

questiontext.text:
Observe the transverse sections of dicotyledonous and monocotyledonous stems shown below:

Anatomical comparison of transverse sections of a typical young dicotyledonous stem and a monocotyledonous stem reveals that:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Compare hypodermal differentiation
In dicot stems, the hypodermis is collenchymatous, providing tensile elasticity. In monocot stems, the hypodermis is sclerenchymatous, providing rigid mechanical support.

Step 2: Compare cortical layers and endodermis
In dicot stems, the cortex is differentiated into hypodermis, parenchymatous cortical layers, and an innermost starch sheath (endodermis). In monocot stems, the ground tissue is undifferentiated into cortex, endodermis, pericycle, or pith.

Step 3: Compare vascular bundle arrangement and structure
In dicot stems, vascular bundles are arranged in a regular ring, are conjoint, open with intrafascicular cambium, and possess endarch protoxylem. In monocot stems, vascular bundles are scattered throughout the parenchymatous ground tissue, smaller peripherally, conjoint, closed (lacking cambium), and surrounded by a sclerenchymatous bundle sheath.

Step 4: Compare phloem parenchyma and vascular cavities
In dicot stems, phloem parenchyma is present and medullary rays occur between bundles. In monocot stems, phloem parenchyma is completely absent, and protoxylem disintegration results in water-containing cavities.

Step 5: Conclude the correct comparative anatomical statement
Dicot stems feature a collenchymatous hypodermis, a starch-rich endodermis, and a ring of open vascular bundles, whereas monocot stems exhibit a sclerenchymatous hypodermis, scattered closed vascular bundles with bundle sheaths, and lack phloem parenchyma.

answer.text: Dicot stems possess a sclerenchymatous hypodermis and scattered closed vascular bundles, whereas monocot stems possess a collenchymatous hypodermis and ringed open vascular bundles.

Dicot stems feature a collenchymatous hypodermis, a starch-rich endodermis, and a ring of open vascular bundles, whereas monocot stems exhibit a sclerenchymatous hypodermis, scattered closed vascular bundles with bundle sheaths, and lack phloem parenchyma.
Dicot stems lack an endodermis and medullary rays, whereas monocot stems contain a well-differentiated cortex, pericycle, and conspicuous medullary rays.
Both dicot and monocot stems possess open vascular bundles with intrafascicular cambium, undergoing identical secondary growth.
